Miss
mis
v.t. & v.i. (to fail of hitting; to perceive the absence of)
Old English missan, to fail to hit. The Authorized Version uses both senses, and the second — to miss a person, to notice a seat is empty — carries one of the most affecting scenes in the friendship of David and Jonathan.

Biblical Definition

The first sense is marksmanship, and it produces one of Scripture's most startling statistics: among Benjamin there were “seven hundred chosen men lefthanded; every one could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss” (Judges 20:16). The second sense is relational and it governs 1 Samuel 20. David asks Jonathan to cover for him: “If thy father at all miss me, then say, David earnestly asked leave of me that he might run to Bethlehem his city” (1 Samuel 20:6), and Jonathan answers with the sentence that sets the whole test: “To morrow is the new moon: and thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty” (1 Samuel 20:18). An empty seat at a feast is what exposed Saul's murderous intent. The word can also mean simply gone: David's men had protected Nabal's shepherds so that “neither was there ought missing unto them, all the while they were in Carmel” (1 Samuel 25:7). To miss, in Scripture, is to register an absence — of a mark, of a man, of a thing entrusted.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines miss as to fail of reaching or hitting; to fail of obtaining; and also, to perceive the want of, to discover something to be lost.

expand to see more

MISS, v.t. To fail of hitting, reaching, finding or obtaining; as, to miss the mark.

MISS, v.t. To discover to be unexpectedly wanting; to perceive the want of; as, I missed my purse.

MISS, v.i. To fail to hit; to fly wide; to deviate from the true direction.

MISS, n. Loss; want; as, the miss of a friend; also, mistake; error.

ABSENCE, n. A state of being at a distance in place; the want or non-existence of a thing in a place.

Key Scripture

Judges 20:16 — "Among all this people there were seven hundred chosen men lefthanded; every one could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss."

1 Samuel 20:6 — "If thy father at all miss me, then say, David earnestly asked leave of me that he might run to Bethlehem his city: for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the family."

1 Samuel 20:18 — "Then Jonathan said to David, To morrow is the new moon: and thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty."

1 Samuel 25:7 — "And now I have heard that thou hast shearers: now thy shepherds which were with us, we hurt them not, neither was there ought missing unto them, all the while they were in Carmel."

Modern Corruption

Absence is easily treated as neutral, a matter of private convenience, where Scripture makes the empty seat evidence — of a friendship, of a danger, and of where a man's allegiance actually lies.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation is to think that absence costs nothing and signifies nothing — that a place unfilled at a table, a gathering or a Lord's Day assembly is a private matter with no message in it. 1 Samuel 20:18 assumes the opposite as a matter of course: thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty. Jonathan does not have to explain why an empty seat will be noticed; in a household, a covenant or a congregation it always is. The whole plot of the chapter turns on the fact that being missed is inevitable and revealing.

The other sense supplies the sharper warning. The Hebrew for sin is built on the idea of missing a mark, and Judges 20:16 gives the picture in its clearest form: seven hundred men who could sling at a hair breadth and not miss. Precision is possible, the target is real, and failure to hit it is failure however sincere the throw. That is exactly what Scripture means by sin — not merely bad intent but an actual missing of the glory of God — and it is why the remedy has to be an imputed righteousness rather than a better aim.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chata (H2398), to miss the mark, hence to sin; paqad (H6485), to visit, to miss or muster; req (H7387), empty; adar (H5737), to be lacking.

expand to see more

Hebrew chata (H2398) — to miss the mark; the same root that gives the Hebrew word for sin.

Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to number, to miss; if thy father at all miss me.

Hebrew req (H7387) — empty, vain; thy seat will be empty.

Hebrew adar (H5737) — to be lacking, to fail; neither was there ought missing unto them.

Greek hamartano (G264) — to miss the mark, to err, to sin; all have sinned and come short.

Usage

"“Could sling stones at an hair breadth, and not miss” — the mark is real."

"“Thou shalt be missed, because thy seat will be empty” — absence speaks."

"“Neither was there ought missing unto them” — a trust honestly kept."
